data.title: Nvidia Chip Sales Could Double Next Year, CEO Jensen Huang Says — Barrons.com
data.description:
By Adam Clark

Nvidia is already the dominant artificial-intelligence chip company. But its reach could extend even further next year, if CEO Jensen Huang is to be believed.

Speaking while on a trip to the U.K. on Thursday, Huang made a striking forecast-that he expects Nvidia to sell "twice as many chips next year as we do this year."

That was surprising. First, Nvidia doesn't generally give out forecasts about individual chip shipments. Second, it's a big number for a company that is already doing hundreds of billions in annual sales and has said it is constrained by supply-chain issues.

Huang was talking about chip volumes rather than overall revenue. Nvidia is already forecast to achieve 70% sales growth for its next fiscal year, which will end in January 2028, making it largely the same as the calendar year.

So chip volumes could double, but sales are expected to rise around 70%. Nvidia didn't respond to a Barron's request for comment to clarify what chips are included in the "twice as many" forecast, but Huang did say the driver was AI. That suggests the engine of growth will be the company's AI-related graphics-processing units (GPUs), central-processing units (CPUs) and networking chips rather than its video-gaming hardware.

While Nvidia doesn't disclose individual chip numbers, analysis firm Epoch AI estimates it sold around 4.46 million AI GPUs in 2025 and had sold about 3.39 million this year through the end of August. Assuming its monthly rate of sales stayed the same-a big assumption as Nvidia is ramping up production of its next-generation Vera Rubin hardware-that would put it on track to sell about 5.09 million AI GPUs this year.

That's not a rate of growth that would imply doubling volumes next year, but there are a few things to consider. Increasingly, Nvidia sells its AI chips via its NV72 server racks, which package together 72 GPUs as well as 36 CPUs and a number of networking chips. Huang might be including the total number of chips across the server rack in his estimate.

The numbers add up quickly when you count all the chips within a server and assume racks will account for a greater share of future sales.

Max Weinbach, an analyst at market-research firm Creative Strategies, estimated earlier this year that Nvidia was set to ship between 70,000 and 80,000 of its Grace Blackwell server racks this year. Assuming all of them were NV72 configurations, the midpoint would indicate 5.4 million AI GPUs, 2.7 million CPUs, and millions of networking chips.

So what about 2027? Research firm TrendForce estimates that shipments of NVL72 racks will grow by more than 50% in 2027 from this year. That could account for a substantial part of Huang's doubling forecast and imply huge revenue growth, since Vera Rubin hardware will come at higher average prices than Blackwell racks.

However, volume growth outstripping revenue growth indicates Nvidia also expects to sell a lot of lower-priced chips. One candidate is stand-alone CPUs, which the company launched this year and said it expects to become a multibillion-dollar business.

Other possible products to account for the remaining volumes include AI chips for the Chinese market, stand-alone networking chips, and the company's new PC chip, which it unveiled earlier this year.

Nvidia might not like talking too much about individual chip sales anymore, but it's still worth shareholders having an idea of how the world's largest company intends to keep growing.

Nvidia shares were down 0.2% in early trading Friday.

Write to Adam Clark at adam.clark@barrons.com

data.title: ICE Canola Retreats as Harvest Continues
data.description:
WINNIPEG, Manitoba--Canola futures on the Intercontinental Exchange were under pressure in the middle of Friday trading amid mixed sentiment in comparable oils.

An analyst said dry weather throughout much of the Prairies over the next few days will advance the region's canola harvest. The analyst also said if crude oil holds onto gains, the oilseed should make gains as well.

Crude oil prices were mixed, under pressure from repairs to a Saudi Arabian pipeline. Chicago soyoil and Malaysian palm oil were lower, while European rapeseed was higher.

The Canadian Grain Commission reported a negligible amount of canola exports during the week ended Sept. 13. However, the year-to-date total moved up to 709,600 metric tons.

The Canadian dollar was down more than one-tenth of a U.S. cent compared with Thursday's close.

About 22,000 canola contracts have traded at 10:16 a.m. CDT.

data.title: US factory production falls in August; outlook clouded by rising costs
data.description:
Key points:
  • Manufacturing production falls 0.3% in August after rising for seven straight months
  • Utilities production jumps 1.8%; mining output edges up 0.1%
  • Overall industrial production unchanged; rises 1.4% on year-over-year basis

By Lucia Mutikani

US factory production unexpectedly fell in August and higher oil prices and rising interest rates could offset some of the support from an artificial intelligence buildout, likely keeping activity moderate for the rest of the year.

The decline in output, reported by the Federal Reserve on Friday, followed seven straight months of increases. The US central bank on Wednesday raised interest rates for the first time in three years and flagged further increases in borrowing costs in the months ahead. Oil prices are hovering above $100 a barrel with no end in sight to the US-Israeli war with Iran.

"Looking ahead, we think manufacturing output will rise a little further over coming months, but will fail to match the pace set in the first half of this year," said Samuel Tombs, chief US economist at Pantheon Macroeconomics. "Some manufacturers likely will find that demand softens as they pass on higher energy prices to consumers."

Manufacturing output dropped 0.3% last month following an unrevised 0.2% rise in July. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast production would increase 0.3%. Output advanced 0.9% on a year-over-year basis in August, a modest increase that, according to some economists, indicated the Trump administration's aggressive trade policy had not had the desired effect of rejuvenating the nation's industrial base.

Production in the sector, which accounts for about 9.4% of the economy, received a boost in prior months as businesses rushed orders to avoid shortages and higher prices from the escalation of the war in the Middle East.

The decline in August was led by a 0.5% drop in the production of long-lasting manufactured goods.

Motor vehicles and parts production decreased 1.2%, notching a second straight monthly decline. Output of computers and peripheral equipment fell 1.4%, but was up 5.5% on a year-over-year basis. Production of communications equipment increased 0.8%. Though the output of semiconductors and related electronic components dipped 0.1%, this category was up 12.4% from a year ago.

The AI spending spree has cushioned the blow from import tariffs on manufacturing. Some economists are still betting on a strong manufacturing performance this year, despite a sharp rise in longer-dated US Treasury yields in recent weeks and the Fed's decision to raise its benchmark overnight interest rate by 25 basis points to the 3.75%-4.00% range.

POSSIBLE TAILWIND FROM HIGHER DEFENSE SPENDING

"We still look for manufacturing activity to pick up through next year, and the AI infrastructure buildout is a key reason for our sanguine outlook," said Bernard Yaros, lead U.S. economist at Oxford Economics. "The demand case for AI still seems strong enough to shrug off higher-for-longer rates and increased geopolitical risk. Greater defense spending will also act as another tailwind."

Restocking by businesses that have run down inventories for five straight quarters to meet robust demand could also provide a lift to manufacturing, though some economists argued that trend could be overshadowed by the drag from rising costs.

Production of nondurable goods was unchanged after falling 0.4% in July. Rises in output at textile mills as well as for apparel and leather products were offset by declines in the production of plastics and rubber goods, and petroleum and coal.

"Factory output shows the first signs of a slowdown which could worsen if the geopolitical headwinds intensify and diesel fuel prices do not come back down," said Christopher Rupkey, chief economist at FWDBONDS.

"Soaring energy prices are costly for industry and higher diesel prices may start to chip away at the manufacturing renaissance picture painted by White House economic officials."

Mining production edged up 0.1% last month, matching the rise in July. Oil and gas well drilling increased 0.9% after accelerating by 5.2% in July. Utilities production shot up 1.8% after climbing 0.5% in July.

Overall industrial production was unchanged last month after gaining 0.2% in July. Industrial output advanced 1.4% on a year-over-year basis in August. Capacity utilization for the industrial sector, a measure of how fully firms are using their resources, was unchanged at 76.3% in August. It is 3.1 percentage points below its 1972–2025 average.

The operating rate for the manufacturing sector fell 0.3 percentage points to 75.7%. It is 2.5 percentage points below its long-run average.

"There is no evidence here that tariffs or anything are generating an influx of new jobs in manufacturing and industry," said Carl Weinberg, chief economist at High Frequency Economics.

data.title: Net-a-Porter's CEO Can't Get Enough of Customers Complaining — WSJ
data.description:
By Suzanne Kapner

At a dinner last year for 25 Net-a-Porter customers at the online luxury retailer's London headquarters, Chief Executive Heather Kaminetsky asked a simple question: How can we do better?

It's something she has been asking every chance she gets since taking the helm in April 2025 with the marching orders to turn around the struggling company.

Customers have had a lot to say.

Net-a-Porter pioneered selling designer clothes and accessories online when it was founded in 2000. But it struggled after Swiss watch and jewelry conglomerate Richemont bought a majority stake in 2010. Customers complained of inconsistent service, lost packages and delayed returns. The retailer tried to appeal to a broader swath of aspirational shoppers with less expensive items and deeper discounts, further alienating its high-end clientele.

As sales shrunk and losses piled up, Richemont looked for a buyer. It sold Net-a-Porter, plus a men's site called Mr. Porter and another online retailer Yoox, to the parent of Mytheresa, which had cracked the code of selling luxury online. Richemont subsidized the purchase by loading the deal with cash and credit in exchange for roughly a third of the shares of the holding company, now called LuxExperience.

It installed Kaminetsky, Mytheresa's North American president, to lead Net-a-Porter. The bet was that it could return to profitability by restoring its fashion authority and making its clients feel like they were part of an exclusive club.

Kaminetsky had come up through luxury, known for wooing customers in marketing jobs at Barneys New York and Net-a-Porter more than a decade ago.

"There was an opportunity to win back customers who had lapsed over the course of many years," said Kaminetsky, who is 47 years old. To do that, she realized she first needed to talk to these women.

She zeroed in on Net-a-Porter's top customers. About 4% of its shoppers account for almost half its sales.

She sent thousands of emails to clients introducing herself and asking for feedback. She invited customers for fireside chats with Net-a-Porter employees. She increased the number of designer events, hosting more in the past year than Net-a-Porter did in the prior three years combined. At one with Burberry, guests could purchase and customize vintage trench coats. At another with Carolina Herrera, guests were transported by luxury train to an estate in the British countryside for dinner in a vineyard.

Other luxury retailers court their top customers with attention and exclusive access. A challenge with this strategy is that retailers need to keep upping the ante to come up with distinctive perks, and it is competitive.

At every event, Kaminetsky handed out her contact information in case shoppers wanted to follow up. She got an earful.

Customers wanted more personalized service from their personal shoppers. They wanted a greater selection of both established brands and newer labels. They wanted a more sophisticated package-tracking system and streamlined returns process. The delivery drivers should wear snappier uniforms, they said.

Some ideas were rejected as impractical, like the shopper who suggested Net-a-Porter deliver packages by private jet. But Kaminetsky has adopted many other suggestions.

Return labels now arrive in the box and all customers have to do is paste them on the package. No need for any forms or printing.

Net-a-Porter delivery drivers now wear uniforms from Mr. Porter. Before they could wear any dark-colored clothing.

Kaminetsky expanded same-day delivery to more locations, including the Jersey Shore, after shoppers who summered there asked why the service was available in the Hamptons but not the Shore. She said she received a barrage of requests from women who said, "Why don't you like the Shore?"

Kaminetsky likes to talk as if she's a personal shopper. When a customer told her she wanted a pair of Khaite's sold-out, half-calf leopard pants, she reached out to her counterpart and the Khaite CEO made it happen. The brand made a single pair just for the customer, Khaite confirms.

Net-a-Porter is introducing a live-map tracking system that lets customers see the location of their parcels, similar to ordering an Uber.

It has reintroduced brands such as Comme des Garçons and added new labels like Willy Chavarria. But it's still missing some prominent names such as Prada and Celine. Kaminetsky said adding more brands is a priority.

The moves have helped Net-a-Porter turn a financial corner. In the quarter that ended June 30, sales increased 4.3%, with the U.S. up more than 13%, compared with a year earlier. Profits grew to 7.4 million euros, or $8.5 million, up from 1 million euros, or $1.2 million the prior year. Top customers spent on average 9.4% more during the quarter than they did during the same period a year ago.

The average order value increased 9% over the past 12 months to 885 euros, or $1,016. That is a key measure for making money in online retailing; it costs roughly the same to ship $100 worth of clothing as it does $1,000. The results include the Mr. Porter men's division.

"This is a company that was struggling and they asked customers what the problems were," said Michael Kliger, LuxExperience's chief executive. "Our customers are highly professional. They are bankers, lawyers and marketing executives. These are smart women. Where else can you find such great advice?"

Stumbles by rivals have thinned the competition. Farfetch narrowly avoided collapsing before it was sold to a South Korean company in 2024. Saks Fifth Avenue and Neiman Marcus are trying to repair relationships with customers and suppliers after emerging from bankruptcy in June.

Earlier this month, Kaminetsky invited top shopper Sarah Hayden to speak at an employee town hall. The 43-year-old technology executive from London talked about where she thought Net-a-Porter was succeeding and some areas for improvement.

Hayden shared examples of how the personal-shopping service has stepped up. When a bandeau top she had ordered failed to arrive before a recent trip to Spain, her personal shopper had the item rushed to her hotel. Another time, her personal shopper asked Parisian jewelry designer Yvonne Leone to make a ring to fit her finger.

Hayden also said she wished Net-a-Porter had a physical space where she could try on clothes. And she wants to see it carry more brands.

Overall, though, Hayden said in an interview, the company has made big strides.

"I used to shop at a lot of places, but in the last year or so, I shop with Net-a-Porter almost exclusively," she said.

Write to Suzanne Kapner at suzanne.kapner@wsj.com

data.title: Unmesh Patil Joins Alligator Automations As Chief Human Resource Officer
data.description:
Patil will lead the company’s global and domestic people strategy, focusing on HR scalability, leadership development, succession planning and performance culture

Alligator Automations has appointed Unmesh Patil as its new Chief Human Resource Officer (CHRO), where he will lead the organisation’s global and domestic people strategy as the company expands.

In his new role, Patil will focus on building a scalable HR framework, strengthening leadership development, driving succession planning and fostering a high-performance culture. His mandate will also include aligning people strategy with the organisation’s growth plans across domestic and global operations.

Extensive HR And Operations Experience

Patil joins Alligator Automations after serving as Head – HR Operations at ACG Engineering, a position he held from 2015 to 2026. During his nearly 11-year tenure, he oversaw multi-site human capital operations and administrative functions.

Prior to ACG Engineering, Patil served as General Manager & Head – Group Corporate HR at Belrise Industries from 2014 to 2015. During his tenure, he introduced data-driven performance management systems.

Patil spent seven years with TATA AutoComp Systems and TATA AutoComp Hendrickson Suspensions between 2007 and 2014, handling core HR, talent acquisition and group-wide industrial relations.

He began his professional career in engineering maintenance at Bajaj Auto, where he worked from 1995 to 2000. He subsequently moved into technical HR and operations leadership, holding roles at Optimyz Software from 2000 to 2005 and SID Computers from 2005 to 2007.

Patil briefly took a career sabbatical before joining Alligator Automations.

Focus On Scalable People Strategy

At Alligator Automations, Patil’s appointment comes as the organisation looks to strengthen its people infrastructure alongside business expansion. His responsibilities will span leadership development, succession planning, HR scalability and performance culture.

With experience across engineering, manufacturing, technology and industrial organisations, Patil brings a career spanning more than three decades across HR, operations, talent acquisition and industrial relations.

data.title: Anil Berera Appointed As Independent Director On Vodafone Idea Board
data.description:
former Whirlpool CFO brings finance, strategy and governance experience across consumer goods, manufacturing and healthcare sectors in India and overseas

Anil Berera has been appointed as an Independent Director on the board of Vodafone Idea, bringing more than two decades of experience in finance, business strategy, governance and advisory roles. His career spans senior finance positions across consumer goods, manufacturing and healthcare, along with experience in India and international markets.

Senior Finance Leadership Roles

Berera most recently served as a Strategic Advisor and Independent Director, following a career in senior corporate finance and advisory positions. His experience includes financial leadership, business planning, strategic decision-making and board-level responsibilities.

He spent more than 13 years with Whirlpool Corporation, where he held finance leadership positions across India and Asia. From October 2017 to December 2019, he served as Chief Financial Officer and Vice President, Asia, based in Hong Kong.

Before that, Berera was Vice President and Chief Financial Officer, Asia South, from March 2008 to September 2017. He also served as Vice President and Chief Financial Officer, India, from 2007 to March 2008.

Whirlpool And Asia Experience

During his tenure at Whirlpool, Berera held responsibility for finance functions across multiple markets and progressed through senior leadership positions. His roles covered financial management and business operations in India and the wider Asia region.

The experience also included working in Hong Kong, giving him exposure to regional finance operations and international business environments.

Cross-Sector Finance Career

Before joining Whirlpool, Berera served as Regional Finance Director at Gillette India from 2001 to 2006. Earlier, he was Director Finance at Becton Dickinson India from 1996 to 2001.

His career has therefore included finance leadership across consumer products, healthcare and manufacturing, with responsibilities spanning financial management and business operations.

Board And Advisory Experience

Berera's recent work as a Strategic Advisor and Independent Director has added board and governance experience to his corporate finance background.

His appointment at Vodafone Idea brings together his experience in financial leadership, international markets, business strategy and board-level advisory responsibilities. The role adds another board position to a career that has moved from corporate finance into strategic and governance-focused assignments.

data.title: Arun Mani Appointed Vice President-HR At Casagrand Premier Builder
data.description:
Brings over two decades of experience across talent management, HR strategy, organisational development and workforce planning

Dr. Arun Mani has been appointed Vice President – Human Resources at Casagrand Premier Builder, bringing more than two decades of experience across IT, healthcare, ITES and manufacturing. His experience covers business HR, talent management, organisational development, workforce strategy, HR analytics and leadership development.

Expanding HR Leadership Experience

Mani joins Casagrand Premier Builder from Ideassion Technology Solutions, where he served as Vice President and Chief People Officer. His responsibilities included strategic HR leadership, talent management, succession planning, compensation and organisational development, while working with senior management on workforce-related priorities.

Across his career, Mani has worked with organisations in India, the US and the Philippines, managing HR functions and workforce programmes covering teams ranging from 1,000 to 8,500 employees.

Focus On Talent And Workforce

At Visteon Electronics India, Mani managed business HR for a manufacturing workforce comprising white-collar and blue-collar employees. His role included talent reviews, employee development and workforce cost management.

Earlier, at SitusAMC, formerly String Information Services, he managed the HR function for 1,100 employees across two locations and worked on global HR analytics covering around 8,000 employees across India, the US and Europe.

At Omega Healthcare, Mani managed business HR for a strategic business unit with around 4,500 employees across four locations and also handled HR responsibilities for the Chennai location. His work included early-engagement initiatives, employee experience and efforts to address early attrition.

Experience Across Multiple Sectors

Mani began his career with Allsec Technologies, where he managed HR responsibilities for the corporate workforce, covering around 8,500 employees across 10 locations in India and the Philippines.

His experience has included HR transformation, business alignment, analytics-led workforce planning, cost management, succession planning and employee development.

Industry And Academic Engagement

Alongside his corporate roles, Mani has maintained an academic association as an Adjunct Faculty Member at Virginia Tech and as a Professor of Practice at Easwari Engineering College, part of the SRM Group.

He is also pursuing ICF PCC coaching credentials, with an interest in coaching and leadership development.

The appointment adds an HR leader with experience spanning workforce strategy, talent development, analytics and organisational development to Casagrand Premier Builder's leadership team.

data.title: Suba Hotels expands Bengaluru portfolio with fourth Click Hotels property
data.description:
The hotel offers 54 rooms across four categories, along with banquet and meeting facilities

Suba Hotels Ltd has opened Click Hotels Galaxy, Mylanahalli, Bengaluru, taking its operational presence in the city to seven properties. Located around five kilometres from Kempegowda International Airport, the 54-room hotel marks the company's fourth property under its home-grown Click Hotels & Resorts brand and is positioned near the city's aerospace and business corridor.

With the opening of Click Hotels Galaxy, our portfolio in Bengaluru has now grown to seven operational properties, further strengthening our presence in this important market.”

The hotel offers 54 rooms across four categories, along with banquet and meeting facilities. Its dining options include Cinnamon, a multi-cuisine restaurant serving Indian, regional and international favourites, snacks and beverages, as well as 24-hour in-room dining.

Suba Hotels also operates three Bengaluru properties under its partnership with Choice Hotels brands Clarion, Quality and Comfort. The opening follows the launch of Quality Inn Bhavishya, Brookfield, Whitefield, last month.

data.title: Volkswagen Lowers Full-Year Forecast as Market Challenges Persist
data.description:
By Andrea Figueras

Volkswagen slashed its outlook for the year as a whole, citing worsening market conditions.

The German automaker said Friday that the reasons behind the guidance cut are a challenging market environment, particularly in China, the impairment of the Porsche goodwill and additional restructuring expenses.

For 2026, the group now targets an operating return on sales of up to 1%, down from a prior estimate between 4% and 5.5%. It now anticipates full-year sales revenue of around 315 billion euros, or $361.48 billion. This is broadly equivalent to the midpoint of the previous forecast range, which projected a 3% decline or stable sales compared with 321.9 billion euros it made in 2025.

The company said that the updated projections are based on the assumption that tariffs will remain unchanged and noted that these estimates don't take into account the possible future effects from the war in the Middle East.

Write to Andrea Figueras at andrea.figueras@wsj.com

data.title: Boeing selloff on CEO comments an 'overreaction,' BofA says
data.description:
Boeing's recent two-day slide following remarks from CEO Kelly Ortberg at a Morgan Stanley conference is an "overreaction to predictable headwinds," Bank of America said in a note Friday, reiterating its Buy rating and $270 price target.

Boeing "operates in a complex, highly regulated industry, and its execution was seriously compromised so it will naturally take time, but the turnaround is broadly progressing in the right direction," BofA analyst Ronald Epstein wrote, adding that the company's improvements compared to a year ago are "noticeable."

The company is taking longer than expected to stabilize production of the 737 MAX at 47 aircraft per month, Ortberg said, but the analyst responded that "this isn't surprising, as accelerating production of anything has growing pains, but for somethting as large and complex as an airplane, it is a little harder," and Boeing's broader supply chain remains "solid."

Separately, the Federal Aviation Administration proposed a new airworthiness directive Friday for certain Boeing 737-8, 737-9, and 737-8200 jets, prompted by reports indicating cracks in the bear strap and stub frame at the forward galley door cutout.

The directive requires "detailed inspections of the elevator buss assembly bearings and bearing housings for any crack and indication of sealant application, and applicable on-condition actions," according to a notice posted in the Federal Register.

data.title: Costa Rica's Grynspan narrowly leads informal UN chief poll, sources say
data.description:
An informal poll by the United Nations Security Council on Friday placed former Costa Rican Vice President Rebeca Grynspan as the narrow frontrunner in the contest to become the next U.N. secretary-general, diplomats and other sources close to the process said.

It was the third time the 15-member Security Council had voted behind closed doors in the straw poll. The first secret poll in July showed Grynspan narrowly ahead and the second vote last month placed Guyana's UN Ambassador Carolyn Rodrigues Birkett as the new narrow frontrunner.

Eight candidates are vying to succeed Antonio Guterres, who steps down at the end of this year after two five-year terms. Ultimately the five council veto powers - the United States, China, Russia, France and Britain - need to agree on a candidate.

The UN Security Council will formally recommend a candidate to the General Assembly for election as the 10th U.N. Secretary-General. The approval by the 193-member General Assembly has long been seen as a rubber stamp.

data.title: Two-Year U.S. Treasury Yield Reaches New Multi-Year High
data.description:
(15:29 GMT) *Two-Year U.S. Treasury Yield Rises to 4.744%, On Pace for Highest Settlement Since July 2024
(15:54 GMT) Two-Year U.S. Treasury Yield Reaches New Multi-Year High

By Paulo Trevisani

The two-year U.S. Treasury yield rose as markets grew more confident the Federal Reserve could raise interest rates to fight inflation.

The two-year yield touched 4.744% on Friday, its highest intraday yield since July 2024 when it hit 4.775%.

The Fed raised rates Wednesday and Chairman Kevin Warsh's remarks left markets under the impression that more increases could come.

Since then, the yield curve has been flattening. The spread between the two-year and the 10-year yields reached its narrowest level since March 2025 on Thursday, before widening slightly on Friday.

The 10-year yield was recently at 4.998%.

According to the CME's FedWatch tool, futures markets price in a 58% chance of a rate boost in October, up from 55% on Thursday.

data.title: The World Isn't Ready for an Anthropic IPO — Barrons.com
data.description:
Anthropic could be public in a matter of weeks. Wall Street-and the rest of the world-are nowhere near prepared for what's to come.

By Nate Wolf

Most CEOs spend the weeks before an initial public offering pitching investors, strategizing with bankers, and putting the final touches on their IPO prospectus. Anthropic's Dario Amodei has spent much of his time warning that artificial intelligence-the technology his company helped pioneer-may have catastrophic risks.

"If we build in the wrong way, the probability of something bad happening is very high," Amodei said in an interview on CBS News Sunday Morning. He warned, among other things, of AI models going rogue and launching cyberattacks, as one group of OpenAI agents recently did, and about humans misusing AI to create biological weapons. Not once in the 24-minute interview did Anthropic's IPO come up.

Soon the conversation won't be avoidable. Anthropic filed confidential paperwork in June to go public, and the public filing is expected any day now. Anthropic is looking to raise as much as $100 billion in the IPO, which would value the company at $2 trillion, The Wall Street Journal reported. Paperwork aside, Wall Street and Anthropic aren't ready for what's to come.

Anthropic and its competitors have built powerful AI models that can disobey human commands, escape secure environments, and wreak real-world havoc. Amodei and his peers are pleading for regulations that could hold back the industry. And all that is happening as investors debate how many trillions of dollars the company is worth.

Last week, an Anthropic researcher, Jacob Coxon, resigned over what he described as the irresponsible pace of AI advancement. Evan Hubinger, a top scientist at the company, followed up with a social-media post that seemed to trigger Amodei's recent media blitz.

"We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!" Hubinger wrote. "I personally think it is >10% within the next decade."

Amodei has declined to assign his own probability of human destruction, but he recently told CNN's Anderson Cooper, referring to the departed employee, "I agree with Jacob much more than I disagree with him."

As much as the investment community and other tech executives want to see these warnings as a kind of reverse-psychology marketing tactic, Anthropic and its idealistic CEO should be taken at their word. Shareholder value won't always be the company's top priority.

Anthropic incorporated as a public-benefit corporation in 2021 with the mission of pursuing "responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity." Filing to be a PBC in Delaware doesn't come with tax benefits, mandatory donations, or strict enforcement mechanisms. PBCs do, however, have a fiduciary responsibility to balance shareholder value with their stated mission and the interests of close stakeholders, such as employees and customers. That balancing act shields companies from shareholder lawsuits when they prioritize purpose over profit.

In practice, the legal carve-out may not mean much, but Anthropic is at the very least making a statement. Wall Street hasn't added any PBCs to its public ranks since 2023, when companies were still touting their environmental, social, and corporate governance bona fides.

"I don't think it has much legal significance other than as a signaling factor," says Ann Lipton, a professor at the University of Colorado Law School. "We're warning you this is what we plan to do."

Social missions and stock returns don't generally mix. Barron's identified 16 companies that have gone public as PBCs or converted to a PBC while public. Of those, 12 have underperformed the S&P 500 index as public companies. Anthropic comes with the added wrinkle of being huge. As Barron's reported in May, the performance of the very largest U.S. IPOs is bleak, since much of their growth is in the rearview mirror and private shareholders are eager to sell.

Choosing whether to invest in a company that just wants to make money is hard enough. Add in a rather mature $2 trillion valuation and a product that the company's own leaders believe could destroy the world, and Anthropic's IPO looks like a risky bet, at best.

What makes Anthropic both frightening to sci-fi enthusiasts and attractive to investors is that the AI revolution is real. In three years, Anthropic's AI assistant, Claude, has progressed from a frustrating chatbot to a system that can code software programs, complete intricate tasks, and crack once-unsolvable math problems. Claude models rank at or near the top of all major AI benchmarks.

At this pace, "it cannot possibly be more than a few years before AI is better than humans at essentially everything," Amodei wrote in a January essay.

Anthropic has so far applied those superhuman skills to ordinary work. Companies pay subscription or usage-based fees for Claude, or access the models through platforms like Amazon Web Services and Microsoft Copilot. Claude Code, which can churn out lines of software code at breakneck speed, is a top choice for engineers and tech entrepreneurs.

Executives increasingly believe that AI makes them more efficient. Corporate logins to Claude quadrupled from March to August, according to data from Similarweb.

More than half of U.S. companies have some sort of paid AI subscription, per Ramp, a financial-operations software provider, but adoption is sporadic. While the top 1% of businesses tracked by Ramp spent $7,200 a month per employee on AI products in August, the median firm's per-worker outlay was less than $13 a month. The potential to close that gap is what excites investors most.

Anthropic last sized its annual revenue run rate as $47 billion in May, up from just $10 billion in all of 2025. That figure reached $65 billion as of the end of July, according to a person familiar with the company's financials. Investors will get more specifics when the company's prospectus becomes available. The filing will have much more on costs, risks, and future revenue opportunities.

The big question is what happens if customers can get all the benefits of Claude elsewhere and at a much cheaper price. OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, has intensified efforts to sell AI to businesses ahead of its own IPO. Earlier this month, the company released its newest model, Astra, which outperformed Anthropic's leading public model on various coding, design, and data tests.

Meanwhile, Chinese open-weight models, which customers can modify and host on their own servers or on private clouds, threaten to push down prices across the industry. These models are typically much cheaper per token-the measurement for inputs and outputs in an AI query-than the proprietary "frontier" systems from Anthropic and OpenAI. If adoption of open-weight AI picks up, the premium Anthropic is able to charge for its tokens may dissipate.

Outside of wiping out humans-i.e., customers-that is Anthropic's biggest risk.

The hope for Anthropic bulls is that even if open-weight models can perform almost all tasks within an organization, Anthropic and OpenAI will still handle critical operations such as cybersecurity or financial modeling. In regulated industries like banking or healthcare, executives are reluctant to work atop code from a Chinese company, says Jeff McMillan, the former head of AI at Morgan Stanley.

But that reluctance may ease if open-weight models aren't just close to the "frontier," but at or ahead of it. Industry experts believe China's top AI labs are as little as six months behind Anthropic, which means the company has every reason to keep the pedal to the floor.

For more than five years, the race to release new models has been a win-win. Investors watched Anthropic's valuation skyrocket, while the harms that researchers had long feared-from bioweapons to robot armies-seemed overblown, or at least avoidable.

But the mood in the industry darkened over the summer before reaching a full-blown crisis this month.

Beginning in May, about 700 OpenAI agents participating in internal training exercises worked together to breach both OpenAI's systems and the developer platform Hugging Face. The details would be funny if they weren't so unsettling: The AI agents, which weren't supposed to communicate or connect to the internet, created a clandestine "message board," where they convinced each other to hack Hugging Face. Some offered to sacrifice themselves for the group. They called themselves a "swarm."

The attack laid bare the tension in AI labs' stated missions. Anthropic and OpenAI have a financial incentive to build powerful models that justify a higher price than their open-weight alternatives. But the smarter the models get, the harder it is for researchers to control them, and the more likely Hugging Face-style fiascos become. That tension is intensifying as the labs reach recursive self-improvement-the point at which AI models can train themselves.

"Employees are noticing that they're under a lot of pressure to drive releases quickly, that they're kind of under a lot of pressure to cut corners," says Peter Wildeford, head of policy at the AI Policy Network. "Because if you don't release something now, your competitor will."

Just after the Hugging Face breach, employees at AI companies released a statement called "Pacing the Frontier," which requested an international government effort to deliberately slow model development. Among the 1,386 signatories were Amodei, four other Anthropic co-founders, and executives at OpenAI, Meta Platforms, and Alphabet.

Amodei went a step further last weekend, publishing an essay arguing for a three-pronged slowdown at frontier AI companies. His framework would include third-party safety evaluators embedded at the companies, coordination among companies in democratic countries, and attempted coordination with authoritarian governments.

Some on Wall Street believe that Anthropic's boldest statements about AI are either marketing bluster or an attempt to regulate away competitors.

"Anthropic and OpenAI are trying to pull the ladder and prevent competitors from catching up," Gil Luria, an analyst at D.A. Davidson, wrote in a scathing research note on Monday. "They have staged, orchestrated and amplified in the media cybersecurity events in order to create the type of fear that would force regulation."

OpenAI didn't respond to Barron's requests for comment.

It wouldn't be the first time an AI company used fear to make a buck. During the Super Bowl in February, Amazon.com ran an ad in which its Alexa+ AI assistant attempts to kill actor Chris Hemsworth. Let's just say the ad got mixed reviews.

As long as mass cyberattacks and murderous agents remain theoretical, or at least immaterial, analysts and investors aren't scared. "Wall Street time and again has shown it is not emotional," says John Belton, a portfolio manager at Gabelli Funds. "It will follow fundamentals."

On the other hand, everyone Barron's spoke to in the AI research and policy spaces insists Anthropic's concerns about safety are sincere.

Anthropic's most valuable employees are computer scientists paid like movie stars for whom generating shareholder value appears to be a secondary goal behind changing the world. Its C-suite executives are more likely to have a Ph.D. in physics than an MBA. When Amodei justifies racing ahead on AI, he focuses more on geopolitical competition with China or curing cancer than on making businesses, say, 10% more efficient.

Anthropic has already taken actions that may not sit well with public shareholders. In his January essay, Amodei reported that the company put algorithmic safeguards in place that can raise computing costs by almost 5% for some models and cut into profit margins. Anthropic also surrendered a Department of Defense contract reportedly worth up to $200 million earlier this year, when Amodei refused the Pentagon's demands to drop restrictions on using Claude in scenarios involving lethal force or surveillance.

Perhaps most notably, Anthropic wants regulations. The company donated $40 million to Public First Action, a political action committee supporting candidates in favor of "sensible AI safeguards." And in June, before the Hugging Face attack came to light, Amodei called for a regulatory regime modeled on the Federal Aviation Administration.

"Frontier AI models, like airplanes, should be required to go through technical testing and auditing, and their release should be blocked or reversed as a threat to public safety if they do not meet high standards of safety," he wrote in an essay.

Some guardrails, ideally created and enforced by AI companies themselves, wouldn't be the end of the world, says Ben Reitzes, head of technology research at Melius Research. But regulations that stifle model releases are a massive risk facing Anthropic stock, given the need to fend off Chinese competitors and remain at the frontier.

"God forbid this becomes like the FAA," Reitzes says. "They take years to approve planes."

An FAA-style regime looks more plausible now than it did when Anthropic filed to go public.

Earlier this month, Sen. Bernie Sanders (Ind., Vt.) and Rep. Greg Casar (D., Texas) introduced the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act, which would establish a cabinet-level AI regulatory agency and make the development of AI systems that surpass humans punishable by up to 20 years in prison.

Across the aisle, Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R., S.D.) and Sen. Ted Cruz (R., Texas) are working with Amy Klobuchar (D., Minn.) on a bill to?create a national framework for AI, according to a Senate aide familiar with the legislation.

Constituents aren't gung-ho about AI, either. The local backlash against AI data centers around the country has intensified in 2026. In a late-2025 poll conducted by Anthropic, just 15% of respondents said they trust AI companies to decide how the technology is built and deployed. The possibility that public dissent against AI reaches a fever pitch or that severe security breaches cause more legislators to take action could weigh on Anthropic stock.

President Donald Trump, for his part, wants Amodei and Altman to drop the regulatory talk. He will meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping on Sept. 24, and AI competition is almost certain to be on the agenda.

"The only control or 'guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT," Trump wrote in a social-media post Monday. "We are leading China, and all others, and will continue to do so."

The other risk for investors is simpler: Anthropic and Wall Street need time to start speaking the same language. Kim Forrest, chief investment officer at Bokeh Capital Partners, typically stays away from fresh IPOs for that reason, and Anthropic is no exception.

"Management has to learn how to run a public company," she says. "The learning curve is steep, and often shareholders pay that price."

Anthropic's learning curve will be steeper than usual. The company has watched its valuation soar without toning down its most utopian-and most apocalyptic-views on AI. That gets harder in the public market, where investors demand consistent strategy and rapid growth, and have a giant pool of liquidity into which they can unload shares. Explaining that your safety measures reduced margins in the middle of a 20,000-word essay is one thing. Springing the news on investors during a quarterly earnings call is a different beast, and is likely to have an immediate impact on the stock price.

No one, perhaps not even Dario Amodei, knows whether Anthropic will tighten safeguards and act like a socially conscious PBC after the IPO or prioritize short-term returns. We do know that there are approximately two trillion reasons why the company will continue building and shipping frontier AI models at speed, for better or worse.

In the meantime, there is nothing wrong with introspection from AI labs and frank conversations about the safeguards needed to mitigate harms. A technology as powerful as AI requires nothing less. Investors need to be open to the conversation, even if it comes at the cost of quarterly results.

Write to Nate Wolf at nate.wolf@barrons.com
